mainTopic: A late ערב in the משנה, and the גמרא's question whether a loan's lien on property (שעבוד) comes from the Torah, as argued by עולא and רבה and by רב and שמואל against רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש.
overview: The amud opens with the end of a משנה about collecting debts. A note in the borrower's own handwriting, or a ערב added after the שטר was signed, lets the lender collect only from נכסים בני חורין. בן ננס argues that such a late ערב owes nothing at all, because the lender never lent the money trusting him. רבי ישמעאל then praises money law and tells students to learn it from בן ננס. The גמרא asks whether a loan's lien on the borrower's property (שעבוד) comes from the Torah. עולא says it does, and the חכמים removed it from oral loans to protect buyers. רבה says it does not, and the חכמים added it to written loans so people would keep lending. A ruling of רבה's about a בכור seems to contradict him, and the גמרא answers that he was only explaining בני מערבא. רב and שמואל say an oral loan cannot be collected from heirs or buyers, while רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש say it can. A ברייתא about a pit digger's heirs is used to challenge רב and שמואל, and the גמרא defends them: the digger had already been judged in court before he died.

steps.title: A loan written in the borrower's own handwriting
steps.stepSummary: If the lender holds a note in the borrower's own handwriting, with no witnesses, he can collect only from property the borrower still owns.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the lender shows a paper written by the borrower himself saying he owes money, the lender collects only from the borrower's unsold property.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives another case in its list of how a lender collects: a debt note the borrower wrote himself, with no witnesses signed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A proper שטר signed by witnesses is publicly known, so it puts a lien on the borrower's land. The lender can then collect even from land that was later sold. A note in the borrower's own handwriting is not publicly known, so buyers had no warning. That is why the lender may collect only from נכסים בני חורין.

keyTerms.meaning: His own handwriting: a note the borrower wrote himself, without witnesses
Collects (payment of the debt)
'Free' property: property the borrower still owns, not sold to anyone

steps.confusionAlert: The note is still a valid proof that he owes the money. The limit is only on which property the lender may take: unsold property yes, sold property no.

phrases.english: If he brought out against him his own handwriting
phrases.notes: The lender shows a note that the borrower himself wrote, with no witnesses signed on it.

phrases.english: saying that he owes him money
he collects from unsold property.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוֹצִיא עָלָיו כְּתַב יָדוֹ שֶׁהוּא חַיָּיב לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's list of ways a loan is proven and what property they allow collecting from.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A debt note in the borrower's own handwriting allows collection only from נכסים בני חורין.

steps.title: A guarantor who joins after the document is signed
steps.stepSummary: A ערב whose guarantee was added after the witnesses signed the שטר can be collected from, but only from his unsold property.
steps.simpleTranslation: A guarantor who signs on after the loan document was already signed: the lender collects from him only from property he still owns.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the rule for a ערב whose promise came after the loan document was already finished and signed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The witnesses' signatures cover only what was written above them. A ערב added below the signatures is not covered by that שטר. So his guarantee works like an oral loan or a handwritten note. That means no lien on sold property, only collection from נכסים בני חורין.

keyTerms.meaning: Guarantor: someone who promises to pay if the borrower doesn't
After the signing of the documents, meaning after the witnesses signed

phrases.english: A guarantor who comes out
phrases.notes: Meaning his guarantee shows up in the document below the witnesses' signatures.

phrases.english: after the signing of the documents
he (the lender) collects from unsold property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same 'unsold property only' rule to a new case: a late-added ערב.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ערב added after the שטר was signed is collected from only from נכסים בני חורין.
steps.whyThisMatters: This case of the late ערב is what the rest of the משנה argues about.

steps.title: A real case before רבי ישמעאל
steps.stepSummary: A real case of a late guarantor came before רבי ישמעאל, and he ruled that the lender collects from the ערב's unsold property.
steps.simpleTranslation: A case like this happened and came before רבי ישמעאל. He said the lender collects from the guarantor's unsold property.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה tells a true story to support the rule it just gave about the late ערב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל's ruling matches the rule in step 2. The ערב is obligated, but since his promise is not covered by the witnessed שטר, only his unsold property can be taken. This sets up the argument that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: An incident: a real case that happened
The תנא who ruled on the case

phrases.english: There was an incident, and it came before Rabbi Yishmael,
and he said: He collects from unsold property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the rule of step 2 being applied in a real case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי ישמעאל: the late ערב is collected from, from his נכסים בני חורין.

steps.title: בן ננס disagrees: the late guarantor pays nothing
steps.stepSummary: בן ננס argues that the late ערב owes nothing at all, not from sold property and not from unsold property.
steps.simpleTranslation: בן ננס said to him: He cannot collect at all, not from sold property and not from unsold property.
steps.whatsHappening: בן ננס challenges רבי ישמעאל's ruling and says the late ערב is completely free.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל limited how the lender collects, but agreed the ערב owes. בן ננס goes further and says the ערב is not obligated at all. His reason comes in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who disagrees with רבי ישמעאל here
Property under a lien that has already been sold to others

phrases.english: Ben Nannas said to him:
He does not collect, not from sold property under a lien
and not from unsold property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly disputes רבי ישמעאל's ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ישמעאל's ruling that the late ערב pays from his unsold property.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The late ערב was never truly obligated, so there is nothing at all to collect from him.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל asks why
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל asks בן ננס for the reason behind his view.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Why?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ישמעאל asks בן ננס to explain himself. This line sets up בן ננס's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing new is decided here. The question opens the door for בן ננס to give the reason why a late ערב is completely free.

keyTerms.meaning: Why?

phrases.english: He said to him: Why?
phrases.notes: רבי ישמעאל is the one asking here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind בן ננס's objection.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason the late ערב should be fully exempt.

steps.title: The example of the man stopping an attack
steps.stepSummary: בן ננס brings a case. A man says 'let him go and I'll pay' to someone choking a borrower in the market. He is exempt, because the loan was not given on his trust.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Think of someone choking another man in the market, and a third person comes and says, 'Let him go, and I will pay you.' That third person owes nothing, because the lender did not lend the money trusting him.
steps.whatsHappening: בן ננס answers רבי ישמעאל's question by comparing the late ערב to a bystander who promises to pay just to stop a fight.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ערב is obligated because the lender gave the loan relying on him. The bystander made his promise after the loan already existed. So the lender lost nothing because of him, and the promise is not binding. A ערב added after the שטר was signed is the same: the loan was already given before his promise.

keyTerms.meaning: One who chokes or grabs by the throat
Leave him alone
Exempt, not obligated
Relying on his trust

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic reason a ערב is obligated: the lender lent because he trusted him.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: הֲרֵי הַחוֹנֵק אֶת אֶחָד בַּשּׁוּק,
phrases.english: He said to him: Consider one who is choking someone in the marketplace,
phrases.notes: The lender is grabbing the borrower and demanding his money back.

phrases.english: and another person found him and said to him
'Leave him alone [and I will give you the money]'
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets are added in the corrected wording.

phrases.english: he is exempt,
because the lender did not lend him the money relying on this man's trust.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question 'why?' with a comparison case.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A promise made after the loan was given is not binding, because the loan was not made on that person's trust.

steps.title: Which guarantor is truly obligated
steps.stepSummary: בן ננס finishes his point. The obligated ערב is the one who says 'Lend him, and I will pay you' before the loan is given.
steps.simpleTranslation: So which guarantor does have to pay? One who says, 'Lend him money, and I will pay you.' He must pay, because the lender gave the loan trusting him.
steps.whatsHappening: בן ננס completes his argument by describing the kind of ערב who really is obligated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference is timing and cause. When the promise comes before the loan and leads the lender to lend, the ערב is responsible. A late ערב, like the bystander, does not fit this. So by בן ננס's view he owes nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: Lend him
Obligated
Since, because

steps.whatToRemember: According to בן ננס, a ערב is obligated only when the lender lent money because he trusted the ערב. A promise made after the loan (like a ערב after the שטר was signed) is not binding. רבי ישמעאל holds that he does pay, but only from נכסים בני חורין.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אֵיזֶה הוּא עָרֵב שֶׁהוּא חַיָּיב?
phrases.english: Rather, which is a guarantor who is obligated?
One who says, 'Lend him, and I will give it to you,' is obligated,
since the lender lent him the money relying on this man's trust.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אֵיזֶה הוּא עָרֵב שֶׁהוּא חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite case to the bystander, completing בן ננס's reasoning.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Only a ערב whose promise caused the loan to be given is obligated.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל praises the study of money law
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל says money law is the best path to wisdom and tells people to learn it from שמעון בן ננס.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ישמעאל said: If you want to become wise, study money law. No area of Torah is greater, and it is like a spring that keeps flowing. If you want to study money law, become a student of שמעון בן ננס.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the closing line of the משנה. Right after hearing בן ננס's argument about the late ערב, רבי ישמעאל praises money law and praises בן ננס himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Money law keeps producing new ideas, like water that never stops coming out of a spring. רבי ישמעאל just saw בן ננס's sharp reasoning, so he points students to him as the teacher to learn from.

keyTerms.meaning: will become wise
laws about money and property
area or field of study
a flowing spring that never runs dry
serve a teacher, meaning learn as his close student

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה ends with praise: money law sharpens the mind, and בן ננס is a master of it.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yishmael said:
One who wants to become wise
should busy himself with money law,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין לָךְ מִקְצוֹעַ בַּתּוֹרָה יוֹתֵר מֵהֶן,
phrases.english: for there is no area in the Torah greater than them,
and they are like a flowing spring.
And one who wants to busy himself with money law
should serve Shimon ben Nannas.
phrases.notes: This is the same בן ננס who just argued with him about the late ערב in steps 4-7.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the argument with בן ננס by praising money law and בן ננס himself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Money law is the best path to wisdom, and one should study it under שמעון בן ננס.

steps.title: עולא: by Torah law, every loan reaches sold property
steps.stepSummary: עולא rules that by Torah law both written and oral loans can collect from property the borrower later sold, because the lien is from the Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא. עולא said: By Torah law, a loan with a document and an oral loan can both be collected from property that was sold. Why? Because the lien is from the Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins with a new basic question. Does a loan put a lien on the borrower's land? עולא says yes, by Torah law, for every kind of loan.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A lien means the borrower's land is tied to the debt. Even if he sells the land later, the lender can take it from the buyer. עולא says this tie comes from the Torah itself, so a written document is not what creates it.

keyTerms.meaning: the discussion of the משנה begins here
by Torah law, before any rabbinic changes
a loan written in a signed document
an oral loan with no document
tied-up property: land the borrower sold after taking the loan
the lien that ties the borrower's property to the debt

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read נכסים משועבדים as 'property still owned by the borrower.' It means land he already sold to buyers. The question is whether the lender can take it back from them.
steps.whyThisMatters: Whether the lien is from the Torah or from the חכמים shapes many laws of collecting debts throughout ש״ס.

phrases.english: Gemara
Ulla said:
By Torah law,
both a loan with a document
and an oral loan
collect from tied-up (sold) property.
What is the reason?
The lien is from the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the גמרא with a new basic topic: the source of the lien on property.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: By Torah law, a lien exists for every loan, so both written and oral loans collect from sold property.

steps.title: Why then can oral loans not reach sold property?
steps.stepSummary: עולא asks himself why the חכמים ruled that an oral loan collects only from property the borrower still owns.
steps.simpleTranslation: So why did the חכמים say that an oral loan can only be collected from property the borrower still owns?
steps.whatsHappening: עולא raises a question against his own ruling. This sets up his explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known rule that an oral loan cannot be collected from sold property. If the Torah gives every loan a lien, that rule needs a reason, so עולא must explain why the חכמים limited the Torah's lien.

keyTerms.meaning: but then, so then
why did the חכמים say
free property: land the borrower still owns

phrases.english: So why did they say
that an oral loan does not collect
except from free property?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how עולא's Torah-level rule fits with the known rabbinic limit on oral loans.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason the חכמים stopped oral loans from reaching sold property.

steps.title: To protect buyers from loss
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים limited oral loans so that buyers of land would not lose out.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because of the loss it would cause to buyers.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא answers his own question. The חכמים took away part of the Torah's power to protect people who buy land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If oral loans could reach sold property, a buyer could lose his land to a debt he never knew about. To protect buyers, the חכמים blocked oral loans from collecting from sold land.

keyTerms.meaning: loss
buyers of land

phrases.english: Because of the loss to the buyers.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The חכמים limited oral loans to protect buyers from losing their land.

steps.title: Then written loans should be limited too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that buyers lose out from written loans as well, so those should also be blocked from sold property.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, a loan with a document should also not collect from sold property!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges עולא's reason. If protecting buyers is the concern, a written loan hurts buyers too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A buyer loses his land whether the debt was written or oral. So the reason 'protect the buyers' seems to apply to both, but the חכמים only limited oral loans.

keyTerms.meaning: if so
also

phrases.english: If so,
a loan with a document too!
phrases.notes: He means: a written loan should also be unable to collect from sold property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reason given in step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: עולא's reason that the limit protects buyers.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Buyers lose just as much from a written loan, so the reason should cover written loans too.

steps.title: With a written loan, buyers caused their own loss
steps.stepSummary: With a written loan the buyers are at fault, because they could have found out about it.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, with a written loan, the buyers caused the loss to themselves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends עולא. A written loan is not the same as an oral one, because the buyer could have checked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A written loan is public enough that a careful buyer could discover it before buying. If he did not check, the loss is his own fault. An oral loan is hard to discover even for a careful buyer, so the חכמים protected him only in that case.

keyTerms.meaning: there, in that case
they caused loss to themselves

phrases.english: There,
phrases.notes: 'There' means the case of a loan with a document.

phrases.english: they are the ones who caused the loss to themselves.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 12.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Buyers are equally innocent in written and oral loans.
steps.terutzMaskana: With a written loan the buyer should have checked, so he caused his own loss. Only oral-loan buyers are protected.
steps.whatToRemember: עולא: the lien is from the Torah. The חכמים blocked only oral loans from sold property, because buyers cannot find out about them.

steps.title: רבה: by Torah law, no loan reaches sold property
steps.stepSummary: רבה disagrees. By Torah law no loan, written or oral, collects from sold property, because the lien is not from the Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבה said: By Torah law, both a loan with a document and an oral loan collect only from property the borrower still owns. Why? The lien is not from the Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רבה, who holds the exact opposite of עולא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For עולא, the Torah gives every loan a lien. For רבה, the Torah gives none. On its own, a loan only lets the lender collect from what the borrower still has.

keyTerms.meaning: an אמורא who argues with עולא here
not from the Torah

phrases.english: And Rabba said:
By Torah law,
both a loan with a document
and an oral loan

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ גּוֹבֶה אֶלָּא מִנְּכָסִים בְּנֵי חוֹרִין.
phrases.english: collect only from free property.
What is the reason?
The lien is not from the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite view to עולא's ruling in step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: By Torah law there is no lien, so no loan collects from sold property.

steps.title: Why then can written loans reach sold property?
steps.stepSummary: רבה asks why the חכמים let a written loan collect from sold property.
steps.simpleTranslation: So why did the חכמים say that a loan with a document collects from sold property?
steps.whatsHappening: Like עולא, רבה asks a question against his own view. This sets up his explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In practice, a written loan does collect from sold property. If the Torah gives no lien, רבה must explain why the חכמים added one.

keyTerms.meaning: collects the debt

phrases.english: And why did they say
that a loan with a document collects from sold property?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how רבה's view fits with the known rule for written loans.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason the חכמים let written loans reach sold property.

steps.title: So people will keep lending
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים gave written loans a lien so lenders would not be afraid to lend.
steps.simpleTranslation: So that the door will not be locked in front of people who need to borrow.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה answers. The חכמים created the lien to protect borrowers' access to loans.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a lender could not collect from sold property, he would fear losing his money and would stop lending. Then people who need loans would have nowhere to turn. So the חכמים gave written loans a lien. For עולא, the חכמים took power away from oral loans. For רבה, they added power to written loans.

keyTerms.meaning: lock the door, meaning cut off access
borrowers

steps.whatToRemember: עולא: the lien is from the Torah, and the חכמים removed it from oral loans to protect buyers. רבה: the lien is not from the Torah, and the חכמים added it for written loans to keep lending alive.

phrases.aramaic: כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא תִּנְעוֹל דֶּלֶת בִּפְנֵי לֹוִין.
phrases.english: So that you not lock the door in front of borrowers.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא תִּנְעוֹל דֶּלֶת בִּפְנֵי לֹוִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The חכמים let written loans reach sold property so that lenders keep lending.

steps.title: Then oral loans should also collect from sold land
steps.stepSummary: If the חכמים wanted to protect lenders, they should have let oral loans collect from sold property too.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, an oral loan should also collect from sold property!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבה's reason. If the goal is to keep lenders from being afraid, oral loans should get the same protection as written loans.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה said the lien is only from the חכמים, who made it so people would keep lending. That reason seems to apply just as much to an oral loan. So why did the חכמים give the lien only to written loans?

keyTerms.meaning: If so: if your reasoning is correct
An oral loan, made without a written document
Also, too

phrases.english: If so,
an oral loan too should collect from sold property!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, מִלְוֶה עַל פֶּה נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reason given in Step 16 by applying it to oral loans.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's reason that the חכמים gave a lien so lenders would not be afraid to lend.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The reason should apply to every loan. Limiting it to written loans looks inconsistent.

steps.title: Oral loans are not publicly known
steps.stepSummary: An oral loan has no publicity, so buyers could not find out about it. That would be unfair to them.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it has no publicity.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that an oral loan is not publicly known. A buyer could not discover it, so it would be unfair to take land away from him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים balanced two concerns: helping lenders and being fair to buyers. A written loan is known to people, so a buyer could have checked and found out about it. An oral loan is hidden, so in that case protecting the buyer wins.

keyTerms.meaning: There: in that case
Publicity, literally 'a voice'

phrases.english: There, with an oral loan,
it has no publicity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes the two cases: a written loan is publicly known and an oral loan is not.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Encouraging lending should apply equally to oral loans.
steps.terutzMaskana: The חכמים did not let oral loans collect from sold property, because buyers could not have known about them.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains the well-known rule that a מלוה על פה cannot collect from property that was sold to buyers.

steps.title: רבה's ruling about a בכור seems to contradict him
steps.stepSummary: רבה ruled that a בכור gets a double portion when a debt owed to his father is collected in land. This suggests רבה holds the lien is from the Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רבה really say this? But רבה said: if they collected land, the בכור gets a double portion. If they collected money, he does not!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether רבה really holds that the lien is not from the Torah. It brings another ruling of his that seems to point the other way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בכור gets a double portion only of what his father already owned when he died. If רבה gives a double portion of land collected for the father's debt, he must view that land as already the father's, through the lien. That fits the view that the lien is from the Torah, which is the opposite of what רבה said in Step 14.

keyTerms.meaning: And did he really say? This introduces a contradiction.
They collected a debt
Land
Money, coins
Firstborn son, who inherits a double portion

phrases.english: And did רבה really say this?
But didn't רבה say:
If they collected land, he has a double portion.
phrases.notes: The case is a בכור and his brothers collecting a debt that was owed to their late father.

phrases.english: If they collected money, he does not!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אָמַר רַבָּה הָכִי? וְהָא אָמַר רַבָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from defending רבה's reasoning to questioning whether it really is his view.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's statement in Step 14 that the lien is not from the Torah.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: His בכור ruling treats collected land as something the father already owned, which only makes sense if the lien is from the Torah.
steps.confusionAlert: The בכור ruling never mentions a lien directly. The contradiction comes from what the ruling implies about the land already belonging to the father.

steps.title: Swapping רבה and עולא does not work
steps.stepSummary: One might suggest switching the two opinions, but עולא elsewhere says that by Torah law a creditor collects from inferior land. That shows his original view was quoted correctly.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say: switch רבה's view for עולא's and עולא's for רבה's. But עולא said: by Torah law, a creditor collects from inferior land!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a possible fix, that the names were switched, and then rejects it right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we switched the names, עולא would hold that the lien is not from the Torah. But עולא himself describes how a creditor collects land 'by Torah law,' so he treats collecting from land as Torah law. That matches the view first quoted in his name, so the switch fails.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say: this introduces a suggestion
Reverse, switch around
By Torah law
A creditor
The lowest-quality land

phrases.english: And if you would say: reverse them,
put רבה's view for עולא and עולא's view for רבה,
but didn't עולא say:
by Torah law, a creditor
collects from the lowest-quality land!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא אֵיפוֹךְ דְּרַבָּה לְעוּלָּא וּדְעוּלָּא לְרַבָּה, וְהָא אָמַר עוּלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Suggests an answer to Step 19 by switching the names, then rejects it.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the suggestion to switch the names of רבה and עולא.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: עולא's own statement about Torah-law collection fits only the view first quoted in his name.

steps.title: רבה was only explaining בני מערבא
steps.stepSummary: In the בכור ruling, רבה was explaining the reasoning of בני מערבא, the scholars of ארץ ישראל. He himself does not hold that way.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבה was saying the reasoning of בני מערבא, but he himself does not hold that way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction. The בכור ruling was not רבה's own opinion. He was explaining someone else's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בני מערבא held that a בכור gets a double portion of land collected for a debt. רבה explained why they hold this, but he did not agree with them. So his real view stays as stated: the lien is not from the Torah.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather: introduces the real answer
The reason behind a view
The people of the West, meaning the scholars of ארץ ישראל
He does not hold that view

steps.whatToRemember: רבה holds that a loan's lien is not from the Torah. The חכמים gave it to written loans so people would keep lending, but not to oral loans, which are not publicly known. His בכור ruling was only an explanation of בני מערבא's view.

phrases.english: Rather, רבה
was stating the reasoning of the people of the West,
phrases.notes: He means the scholars of ארץ ישראל, whose view on the בכור was quoted earlier in this מסכת.

phrases.english: but he himself does not hold that way.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא רַבָּה טַעְמָא דִּבְנֵי מַעְרְבָא קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the switch in Step 20 fails, gives the real answer to the contradiction in Step 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attribution: the conflicting statement was an explanation of another view, not רבה's own opinion.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבה's בכור ruling shows he holds that the lien is from the Torah.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבה was only explaining בני מערבא. His own view is that the lien is not from the Torah.
steps.whyThisMatters: This teaches a common move in the גמרא: an אמורא may explain a view he does not accept, so not every statement in his name is his own ruling.

steps.title: רב and שמואל: an oral loan cannot be collected from heirs or buyers
steps.stepSummary: רב and שמואל rule that a מלוה על פה cannot be collected from the borrower's heirs or from people who bought his land, because the lien is not from the Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב and שמואל both say: with an oral loan, the lender cannot collect from the heirs or from the buyers. Why? Because a lien on property is not a Torah law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the first side of a disagreement: רב and שמואל say an oral loan cannot be collected from heirs or from buyers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the lien on a borrower's property is only a rabbinic rule, then it only applies to a loan with a written document. An oral loan is only a personal debt of the borrower. Once he dies or sells his land, the lender has nothing to collect from.

keyTerms.meaning: An oral loan, made without a written document
Heirs of the borrower
Buyers who purchased land from the borrower
A lien, meaning the borrower's property is tied to the debt
From the Torah

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean the lender loses his money completely. He can still collect from the borrower himself while he is alive. The question is only about heirs and buyers.

phrases.english: Rav and Shmuel both say:
A loan by oral agreement –
he cannot collect, not from the heirs
and not from the buyers.
What is the reason?
A lien on property is not from the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After discussing whether עולא and רבה hold the lien is from the Torah, the גמרא now brings the basic מחלוקת on this question.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oral loan cannot be collected from heirs or buyers, because שעבוד is not from the Torah.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש: an oral loan can be collected from heirs and buyers
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן and רבי שמעון בן לקיש rule that a מלוה על פה can be collected from both heirs and buyers, because the lien is from the Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן and רבי שמעון בן לקיש both say: with an oral loan, the lender can collect both from the heirs and from the buyers. Why? Because a lien on property is a Torah law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the opposite side: רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש say an oral loan can be collected from heirs and buyers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the reasoning is flipped. If the Torah itself ties a borrower's land to his debt, then a document is not needed for the lien to exist. So even an oral loan follows the property to heirs and to buyers.

keyTerms.meaning: Both of them
Collects the debt
Both... and...

steps.whatToRemember: רב and שמואל say שעבודא לאו דאורייתא, so there is no collection from heirs or buyers for an oral loan. רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש say שעבודא דאורייתא, so the lender collects from both.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ דְּאָמְרִי תַּרְוַיְיהוּ:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish both say:
A loan by oral agreement –
he collects both from the heirs
and from the buyers.
What is the reason?
A lien on property is from the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ דְּאָמְרִי תַּרְוַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This gives the opposing view to רב and שמואל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oral loan is collected from both heirs and buyers, because שעבוד is from the Torah.

steps.title: Challenge from the case of a pit digger whose heirs must pay for the ox
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that if an ox fell into a pit and died, the heirs of the pit's owner must pay for the ox. This looks like collecting a debt with no document from heirs, which goes against רב and שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged this: If someone was digging a pit in a public place, and an ox fell on him and killed him, the ox's owner is exempt. Not only that, but if the ox died, the heirs of the pit's owner must pay the ox's value to its owner!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב and שמואל from a ברייתא where heirs must pay for damage their father caused.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pit digger owed money for the ox, but there was no document. That debt is just like an oral loan. Yet the ברייתא makes his heirs pay, which seems to show that such a debt can be collected from heirs, against רב and שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: They raised an objection, usually from a ברייתא
The public domain, a public area
A pit, one of the main categories of damage
Exempt, does not have to pay
Not only that, but even more

steps.confusionAlert: Two different people are involved here. The digger died in the pit, and the ox's owner is exempt for that. The digger's heirs must still pay for the ox.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
One who was digging a pit in the public domain,
and an ox fell on him and killed him – the ox's owner is exempt.
phrases.notes: The ox fell into the pit on top of the digger. The digger is the one at fault for making the pit.

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא עוֹד, אֶלָּא שֶׁאִם מֵת הַשּׁוֹר –
phrases.english: Not only that, but if the ox died –
the heirs of the pit's owner are obligated
to pay the value of the ox to its owner!
phrases.notes: Paying for damage has no document behind it, so it is like an oral loan. That is why this is hard for רב and שמואל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This attacks the view of רב and שמואל from Step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב and שמואל's rule that a debt with no document cannot be collected from heirs.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Payment for damage is a debt with no document, like an oral loan. Yet the ברייתא makes the heirs pay it.

steps.title: The pit digger had already been judged in court
steps.stepSummary: רבי אילעא, quoting רב, explains that the ברייתא is talking about a case where the digger stood trial before he died. A court ruling makes the debt like a loan with a document.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אילעא said in the name of רב: The ברייתא is talking about a case where he stood trial.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers the challenge: the heirs pay only because the court had already ruled against their father before he died.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A court ruling makes the debt public and official, just like a loan with a written document. So the ברייתא is not a case of an oral debt at all. רב and שמואל's rule about oral loans stays in place.

keyTerms.meaning: Stood trial, was judged in court
A loan with a written document

phrases.english: Rabbi Ela said in the name of Rav:
It is talking about when he stood trial.
phrases.notes: The digger was judged before he died. A court ruling makes the debt like a loan with a document.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אִלְעָא אָמַר רַב בְּשֶׁעָמַד בַּדִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This answers the challenge of Step 24 by narrowing the case of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to describe an ordinary damage debt with no document, collected from heirs.
steps.terutzMaskana: The digger had already been judged in court, which makes the debt like a loan with a document. So it can be collected from heirs even according to רב and שמואל.

steps.title: But the ברייתא says the ox killed him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב's answer. The ברייתא says the ox killed the digger, so there was no chance for a trial before he died.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the ברייתא says the ox 'killed him'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from Step 25 by pointing to the wording of the ברייתא itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's answer needs the digger to be alive long enough to stand trial. But the ברייתא says the ox killed him when it fell, which sounds like he died on the spot. If so, there was no court ruling, and the debt is back to being a plain unwritten debt.

keyTerms.meaning: It killed him (the ox killed the pit-digger)
It is taught / the text says

phrases.english: But it is taught: 'it killed him'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of רבי אילעא in Step 25 using the ברייתא's wording.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that the digger stood trial before he died.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the ox killed him right away, there was no time for a trial, so the answer does not fit the ברייתא.

steps.title: The ox left him fatally wounded, not dead on the spot
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אהבה explains that 'killed him' means the ox made him a טרפה, someone with a fatal wound who is still alive for a while.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אדא בר אהבה said: It means the ox made him a טרפה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אדא בר אהבה answers the challenge by reading 'killed him' in a softer way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A טרפה is someone with a wound that will kill him, but not instantly. The ברייתא calls this 'killed him' because death is certain. Meanwhile he was still alive, so there was time to bring him to court and rule against him.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who gives this answer
Someone with a fatal wound who will die from it, but not right away

phrases.english: Rav Adda bar Ahava said:
That it made him a tereifa.
phrases.notes: The ox wounded him so badly he was sure to die from it, but he lived long enough to stand trial.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה: שֶׁעֲשָׂאוֹ טְרֵפָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the wording of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Killed him' means he died instantly, leaving no time for a trial.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Killed him' means he was fatally wounded, so there was time for a trial before he died.

steps.title: Another version says he died and was buried right away
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings רב נחמן's version of the ברייתא, which says the digger died and was buried, so the טרפה answer does not work.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רב נחמן said that a תנא taught: 'He died and it buried him'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges again, this time using a different wording of the same ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, the digger died and was covered over in the pit. That sounds like instant death, not a slow fatal wound. So once again, when could there have been a trial?

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who reports this version of the ברייתא
A תנא taught (a reciter of ברייתות taught it this way)
He died and it buried him

phrases.english: But didn't Rav Nachman say,
a tanna taught: 'He died and it buried him'!
phrases.notes: The ox landing on him in the pit is, in effect, what buried him there.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן, תָּנֵי תַּנָּא: ״מֵת וּקְבָרוֹ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the טרפה answer of Step 27 using a different version of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אדא בר אהבה's טרפה reading, and with it רב's claim that there was a trial.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If he died and was buried at once, there was no living stretch of time in which a court could rule.

steps.title: Judges were sitting right at the pit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that in that version, judges were sitting at the opening of the pit and ruled against the digger before he died.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it is a case where judges were sitting at the opening of the pit, and they ruled him liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא saves רב's answer even for the 'died and buried' version.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if he died very quickly, the court ruled against him in the moments before his death because the judges were right there. So there was still a court ruling, which makes the debt like a loan with a document. רב and שמואל's rule survives: an unwritten debt is collected from heirs only once there was a court ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: There (in that version of the ברייתא)
Judges
At the opening of the pit
They ruled him liable

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב and שמואל, the pit case in the ברייתא is always a case where a court ruled against the digger before he died. That court ruling is what lets the ox's owner collect from the digger's heirs.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not a claim that judges usually sit by pits. The גמרא is setting up a specific case so the ברייתא fits רב and שמואל's rule.

phrases.english: There, it is where judges were sitting
at the opening of the pit, and they ruled him liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם – דְּיָתְבִי דַּיָּינֵי אַפּוּמָּא דְבֵירָא, וְחַיְּיבוּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 28 and keeps רב's answer from Step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case to a specific situation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If he died and was buried at once, no court could have ruled before his death.
steps.terutzMaskana: The judges were right at the pit and ruled before he died, so there was a court ruling after all.
steps.whyThisMatters: It keeps רב and שמואל's rule standing: an unwritten debt cannot be collected from heirs unless there was a court ruling.
